# babymalpractice.com

> babymalpractice.com is a legal resource by The Alvarez Law Firm, based in Coral Gables, Florida, representing families nationwide in catastrophic birth injury cases. The site covers cerebral palsy, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), Erb's palsy and brachial plexus injuries, fetal monitoring failures, vacuum and forceps injuries, defective birth products, hospital and nursing negligence, and infant wrongful death. The firm's medical-legal team pairs Herb Borroto, M.D., J.D. (Medical-Legal Expert) with Alex Alvarez, Board Certified Civil Trial Lawyer (NBTA).

## Main Pages

- [babymalpractice.com — Home](https://www.babymalpractice.com): Catastrophic birth injury lawyers nationwide. Doctors, nurses, hospitals, and defective products held accountable when a preventable mistake harms a baby.

## Injury Types

- [Injury Types Hub](https://www.babymalpractice.com/practice-areas): Every catastrophic birth injury type the firm handles, in one place.
- [Cerebral Palsy](https://www.babymalpractice.com/cerebral-palsy): Cerebral palsy birth injury lawyers. Herb Borroto, M.D., J.D. reads fetal monitor strips and neonatal records to find the moment oxygen deprivation caused the injury.
- [HIE & Birth Asphyxia](https://www.babymalpractice.com/hie-birth-asphyxia): Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy attorneys. Therapeutic hypothermia within 6 hours of life is the standard of care — failure to cool is malpractice.
- [Erb's Palsy & Brachial Plexus](https://www.babymalpractice.com/erbs-palsy-brachial-plexus): Brachial plexus birth injury lawyers. Shoulder dystocia mismanagement and excessive lateral traction during delivery.
- [Fetal Monitoring Failures](https://www.babymalpractice.com/fetal-monitoring-failures): Failure to recognize and escalate non-reassuring fetal heart rate tracings. ACOG Category II and III management.
- [Vacuum & Forceps Injuries](https://www.babymalpractice.com/vacuum-forceps-injuries): Operative vaginal delivery injuries. Skull fractures, intracranial hemorrhage, brain injury from improper instrument use.
- [Defective Birth Products](https://www.babymalpractice.com/defective-birth-products): Product liability claims for defective fetal monitors, vacuum extractors, epidural catheters, and prescription drugs taken during pregnancy.
- [Hospital & Nursing Negligence](https://www.babymalpractice.com/hospital-nursing-negligence): Hospital vicarious liability, understaffed L&D units, failed chain-of-command, negligent credentialing.
- [Infant Wrongful Death](https://www.babymalpractice.com/infant-wrongful-death): When negligence costs a baby's life. Damages available to the family, statute-of-limitations rules, layered claims.

## Resources & Guides

- [Blog](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/): Catastrophic birth injury insights authored by Alex Alvarez and reviewed by Herb Borroto, M.D., J.D.

## Blog & Patient Education

- [Erb's Palsy vs. Cerebral Palsy — How to Tell Them Apart](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/erbs-palsy-vs-cerebral-palsy): Plain-English comparison of two birth injuries that are sometimes confused — Erb's palsy (peripheral nerve injury to the brachial plexus, typically from shoulder dystocia) vs. cerebral palsy (central nervous system injury, usually from oxygen deprivation), how each is caused, how each is treated, and why the legal pictures are different.
- [Category I, II, and III Fetal Heart Rate Tracings — What Each Means](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/fetal-heart-rate-tracings-categories): The NICHD three-tier classification system explained for parents — Category I (normal), Category III (abnormal), and Category II (indeterminate, where most cases are fought). Covers the standard of care for each category and why most birth injury cases turn on whether a Category II tracing was allowed to progress without delivery.
- [HIE and Cooling Therapy — What Every Parent Should Know](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/hie-cooling-therapy-therapeutic-hypothermia): Therapeutic hypothermia for newborns with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy — eligibility criteria (gestational age, evidence of perinatal asphyxia, moderate-to-severe encephalopathy), the 6-hour treatment window, how cooling is delivered (whole-body cooling blanket, target 33.5°C for 72 hours), and what missed cooling means for both the child's outcome and the case.
- [Vacuum Extractor vs. Forceps — When Each Is Used and What Goes Wrong](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/vacuum-extractor-vs-forceps-when-each-is-used): Operative vaginal delivery in plain English — the ACOG indications and prerequisites, when vacuum vs. forceps is preferred, distinctive injury patterns (cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage, skull fracture, intracranial hemorrhage, facial nerve palsy), and the six most common malpractice patterns including sequential use of both devices.
- [Group B Strep Negligence and Newborn Infection Lawsuits](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/group-b-strep-newborn-infection-cases): When CDC/ACOG/AAP screening and prophylaxis guidelines for GBS are not followed — universal screening at 36-37 weeks, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, the 4-hour pre-delivery dose requirement, and newborn observation — early-onset GBS sepsis and meningitis can devastate a newborn. Covers the five negligence patterns and the records that decide the case.
- [Infant Botulism Missed Diagnosis — What the June 2026 Nara Recall Means for Parents](https://www.babymalpractice.com/blog/infant-botulism-missed-diagnosis-nara-recall-june-2026): The June 12, 2026 voluntary recall of all lots of Nara Organics Powdered Infant Formula after three hospitalized infant botulism cases (CA, WA, PA). Covers the recall scope, the clinical picture (constipation, weak cry, floppy movements, drooping eyelids, breathing problems), the standard of care for diagnosis and BabyBIG treatment, and five patterns of missed-diagnosis malpractice — the "feeding problem" misdiagnosis, sepsis-workup tunnel vision, constipation dismissal, BabyBIG administration delay, and untaken food-exposure history — that turn a treatable illness into preventable injury, prolonged ICU stay, mechanical ventilation, or death.
